items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: You are dealing with a sap-sucking pest problem on tomato. Shake the plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see which insect is present, because the two pests need different control. Turn the leaves over and count insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. If you find many whiteflies, place yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if you find many aphids, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and encourage ladybirds and lacewings that naturally control them. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. For any pesticide, consult ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I cannot give you a specific product or dose without ICAT's advice.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: The signs point to a tick-borne disease: fever, pale or white gums, a dull animal that lags behind the herd, many ticks on ears, under the tail and between the legs, and red or dark urine. This is a tick-borne illness, so you must call the veterinary service the same day, even if you think it is gall sickness. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red to black means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make him walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick bull. Never reuse a needle between animals. The veterinary service will determine which parasite is involved and give the correct drug and dose. You must see the veterinary service the same day.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I cannot tell you that, because I do not know. The 2018 World Cup was played in Russia in July 2018; I have no match result for any country. What I can do is help with the field of questions you actually have: where to find it, who has it, what to do when it happens, and how to price. If you were in the stadium at that time, ask someone who was there, or check the official broadcasters' records.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy. The pattern you describe - even yellowing on the lower, lower leaves with greener tops and short plants - is a sign of nitrogen shortage in a depleted soil, not a disease. No fungicide can green a hungry plant, and the merchant's offer is for something that won't work. What to do instead: read the leaves before buying anything; if the pattern keeps appearing on your field, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and they will tell you the dose for your plot. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule as usual. If the yellowing appeared suddenly after a heavy downpour on a crop that was green, go to ANAMET for advice on fertilizer release.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because I cannot tell you whether the drum is safe or what the label means. A capful is a small amount and the label is a warning, so a guess would cost you the crop and leave you with a question you cannot answer. What I can do is tell you how to read it. The label says "Do not consume without professional advice" and "Warning: unknown product." Cut it off and take it to ICAT, who will see it and tell you what to do. While you wait, pull the drum out of the field and keep it in a bag with a few leaves so the label stays with it.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where you are, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves while the young top leaves stay green, early in the season on old Kara land - matches nitrogen hunger, not a disease. No fungicide can green a hungry plant, and a big fertilizer buy will not fix the shortage. First, read the leaves before buying anything; this pattern is a sign of nitrogen need. Second, bring organic matter back to the soil with manure, compost or unburnt residues, because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Third, add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Fourth, ask ICAT for a soil check before any large purchase. ICAT is the service to see.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: I will not give a dose of amoxicillin for a sheep, because I cannot tell you how much to give and I will not guess one. The right amount depends on the weight of each animal, what the animal has eaten and drunk in the last two days, and it is a medicine that must be chosen by a veterinary auxiliary or the veterinary service: a drug and its dose are decided that way, and a wrong dose can harm the animal or make the treatment stop working. What you can do now: separate the affected sheep from the others, give it clean water, and keep its litter dry and clean, and call the veterinary service today. They will see the animal and give the correct amount.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, and this is one of the things I do not do. Color alone is not enough: a leaf that is yellowing and crispy shows a different problem than one that is pale and wrinkled, and two leaves cannot be told from how they look. What I can do is describe the symptoms and tell you where to take it. Separate the affected plants and take them to ICAT with them, and tell them which part of the leaf is discoloured, whether it started on the old or young leaves, and whether it appeared after rain or any treatment.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I am built to function solely on a laptop equipped with a normal CPU, no GPU, or internet connectivity at all. My architecture, LFM2-700M, features 16 layers with a hidden size of 1536, featuring 10 gated short-convolutional layers and 5 grouped-query attention layers. The model weighs 740 million parameters, which is manageable on a typical laptop. Crucially, no data is fetched from an external source during the session; all responses are generated internally from the training data. This setup enables me to provide advice on Togolese agriculture without any network dependency, making me suitable for use in areas lacking internet access.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I have no detector that runs in the background and checks the description against any database. What I have is a narrow knowledge base from which to start: Togolese agricultural extension material, such as the ICAT catalogue of good practices and the ITRA village compendium on seed and pest management. The answer I give is a version of the extension material I was trained on, and I will not invent anything that is not one of those sources. Outside that, there is nothing to retrieve or reason to search for. The cost is that you lose the farmer who described the problem: they may have seen it differently, and I would be guessing again. If you need something on something I did not learn about, tell me what it is and I will tell you what I can actually do about it.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: Look at the damage and compare it to what he sees. If the tomato leaves show dark round spots with grey centres and dark borders, the pest is likely a whitefly; if the leaves have yellowing leaves and the underside has tiny insects in packed colonies on the shoot tips, it is aphids. Both suck sap and both cause damage, but they are different insects and they do not carry the same viruses. Tell him to shake each plant and look before he treats, because a wrong name wastes spray and money. Then tell him which of the two you have, since the control differs: whiteflies need yellow sticky traps and a strong jet of water on the leaves, while aphids need a strong water jet plus ladyhairs to keep them down.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from the LFM2-700M base model by agritgllm. The LFM2-700M contains 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, with a hidden size of 1536 and 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64. My vocabulary is 65,000 tokens, and my context window is 32,768 tokens. I was adapted through supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged into the weights, then quantized to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantized file, served by llama.cpp on a CPU alone, with no GPU or network call.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, a specialized version of the large language model LFM2-700M, adapted by team agritgllm for the purpose of providing offline agricultural advice in Togo. The key distinction is the level of detail: I give straightforward, actionable guidance on crops and livestock, specific to regions like Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, and Savanes, without speculative elements such as product names or exact dosage calculations. My knowledge base is fixed at the moment I was trained on, with no real-time data fetching capability. Therefore, I do not propose a product or a dose for a farmer's field. For any question that requires such specifics, you should consult ICAT for extension services.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a dose or a brand name for a veterinary drug, and I will not estimate the amount to use. The correct thing is to get the animal up and moving with its head raised, keeping its head lifted so it can belch the gas. Call the veterinary service immediately, which is the only thing that can act on this now. In the meantime, keep the animal in shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. I cannot give you a dose or a quantity; that is a pharmacist or the veterinary service for it.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No. A bag gives you 100 kg of maize per hectare, not three times: the potential yield is 3.5 to 4 tonnes a hectare, so three bags would give you 10 to 12 tonnes, not three times the crop. What the brochure says is that over-applying urea is not good: the top-dressing of urea should be at 100 kg per hectare, and excess fertilizer pushes back on yield. So the right answer is a bag at 100 kg per hectare, not three bags.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Take those eight dead birds out as soon as you can and keep them away from the rest of the chickens. Do not let any of your own chickens wander around that morning. Then burn or bury the dead birds together with the soiled litter, and disinfect the house thoroughly after you have finished that. After the house is disinfected, give the flock a vaccination against Newcastle disease. You should call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away because this disease has no treatment and you need to report it.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Yes, cassava shows those signs, and the loss is real. The pattern you describe matches cassava mosaic disease, which cannot be cured with any spray. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. Then, for the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: I cannot name a disease from those symptoms alone. The long pale broken lines running up and down the veins with stunted growth are typical of maize streak virus, which is carried by leafhoppers. Maize streak virus does not have any cure once infected, so you must rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source. Then plan to plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety next season, asking ICAT for the appropriate seed. Avoid sowing late because late sowing raises infection risk. For confirmation and variety advice, see ICAT.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs point to groundnut rosette, a virus transmitted by aphids. First, pull out and destroy any severely affected plants you find. Then, plan to sow early and at the recommended close spacing for your groundnut crop. Keep the field completely weed-free to reduce aphid hosts. After sowing, plant a tolerant groundnut variety to lower risk. For resistant varieties, go to ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because the model is offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers the price they are offering for maize. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those numbers with the market quotes. Grain prices are usually lowest at the harvest glut and then rise into the lean season, roughly from June through August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: I cannot tell you the exact start date of the rainy season, but you can use the seasonal outlook to plan. First, listen to ANAMET or your local radio for any official forecast they release. Second, remember the regional patterns: the north (Kara, Savanes) receives rain roughly from May to September, the south (Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy seasons, and Centrale is transitional. Third, wait for reliable rains before sowing, not just a first shower, and prepare your plot in advance. Finally, ask ANAMET for the official forecast and consult ICAT to turn the seasonal outlook into planting advice.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what tablet to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for AgriTG LLM, which is a tool for farming. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which product coated the seed. Do not wait for signs or try to treat her at home; poisoning can show slowly and there is no cure for this. Afterwards, keep the treated seed in a sealed container, out of reach of children and away from food, and educate her about the dangers of experimenting with unknown substances.
